t.2.11.1: The great king, undeserving of such a fate, lying there in a manner unfit for him, like Yayāti fallen from the world of the gods when his merit was exhausted,
t.2.11.3: You boast, great king, that you are truthful in speech and firm in your vows; why then do you wish to withhold this boon of mine?
t.2.11.2: That woman, the very embodiment of misfortune, her purpose all but won, fearless yet foreseeing danger, once more demanded that same boon.
t.2.11.4: Thus addressed by Kaikeyī, King Daśaratha then replied in anger, as though overcome with agitation for a moment.
t.2.11.5: When I am dead and Rāma, that bull among men, has gone to the forest, alas, ignoble woman, my enemy, Rāma will have been banished to the forest!
t.2.11.7: As he lamented thus, his mind reeling in confusion, the sun went to its setting, and night came on.
t.2.11.6: If I speak this as the truth, it will turn out to be untrue; surely there will be unequalled infamy for me in the world, and humiliation as well.
t.2.11.8: For the king, so afflicted and lamenting, that night of three watches, though adorned with the orb of the moon, did not shine.
t.2.11.9: Then, sighing hotly in the same way, the aged King Daśaratha, his eyes fixed upon the sky, lamented his sorrow like one in deep distress.
t.2.11.11: Having spoken thus to Kaikeyī, the king, with hands joined in supplication, sought once more to appease Kaikeyī and said this to her.
t.2.11.10: I do not wish you to bring on the dawn; see, I have joined my palms in supplication to you. Or rather, depart quickly, for I do not wish to see the pitiless, cruel Kaikeyī, on whose account this great calamity has arisen.
t.2.11.12: O queen, O gracious lady, show favor above all to the king, who is of virtuous conduct, wretched, wholly devoted to you, and whose life is ebbing away.
t.2.11.13: Surely this was spoken by me thoughtlessly, O lovely-hipped one. Grant me your kind favor, young lady, for you are indeed tender-hearted.
t.2.11.14: Though she heard the strange and piteous lament of the king, her husband, pure of heart, his eyes reddened and his voice choked with tears, she, wicked of heart and cruel, did not do as he asked.
t.2.11.15: Then the king, fainting once again, beholding his beloved wife unappeased and speaking contrarily about the banishment of his son, fell senseless and grief-stricken upon the ground.
